catalog_quote: II. SYLLABLES, QUANTITY, ACCENT. (a) Every word contains as many syllables as vowels; eg Tōkẹ, up, above, upon, &c., &c., is not pronounced as if it was one syllable, but, tó-kẹ. (b) The accent of a syllable is the stress of the voice in pronouncing it. The rising accent is denoted by (1), the falling (1). (c) The accent of words containing two syllables is generally on the first. (d) When nouns begin with ï or n, the accent is on the second syllable. (e) Some words are spelled alike but have different meanings; this difference in most cases is indicated by the accent marks.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (explicitly defined as stress) falls on the first syllable of disyllabic words; nouns carrying a noun-class prefix (i-, syllabic n-) are accented on the second syllable, i.e. on the first syllable of the stem. Net effect: stem-initial stress with unstressed class prefixes. Nyländer 1814: 8 states the same prefix rule for 'Bullom' ('When substantives begin with i, u, or a, the accent is on the second syllable').
new_statements.exceptions: 'generally' on the first; homographs distinguished by rising vs falling accent marks (item e), which in hindsight reflects tone rather than stress placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms in a missionary primer; impressionistic 1862 description. The only modern full description (Childs 2025, Language Science Press) has no statement on stress at all and analyses Sherbro as a (residually) two-tone language with grammatical tone in the verb; Pichl 1967 reportedly transcribed five degrees of stress alongside five tone levels. So the placement statement rests on 19th-c. sources and should be catalogued with that caveat.
new_statements.identity_note: White 1862 was written at Good Hope, Sherbro Island (Bonthe area) and describes Sherbro proper (sher1258). Nyländer 1814 'Bullom' is the Bullom Shore variety north of Freetown, which Childs and others identify with Bullom So / Mani (Glottolog bull1247), although Glottolog files the book under sher1258; its matching prefix-accent rule is therefore supporting evidence from a sister language, not Sherbro itself. Childs 2025 covers all surviving Sherbro dialects (Shenge/Kagboro, Bumpeh, Dema, etc.).

sources.citation: Nyländer, Gustavus Reinhold. 1814. Grammar and vocabulary of the Bullom language. London: Ellerton and Henderson, for the Church Missionary Society.
sources.note: p. 8 (scanned text): 'When substantives begin with i, u, or a, the accent is on the second syllable: as, eboll, before; enang, to-day; ukunt, a monkey-apple; nfoh, speech, language.' No general accent rule beyond this. NB 'Bullom' here is the Bullom Shore variety north of Freetown, probably Bullom So/Mani (bull1247) rather than Sherbro proper, though Glottolog files it under sher1258.

sources.citation: Childs, G. Tucker. 2025. A grammar of the Sherbro language (African Language Grammars and Dictionaries 7). Berlin: Language Science Press. 582 pp. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15045985
sources.note: Nothing on word stress/accent anywhere in ch. 2 Phonology (pp. 29-52: vowels, consonants, 2.2 Tone pp. 41-44, syllable structure, rules) or elsewhere in the grammar. Treats prosody as tone: 'historically Sherbro was undoubtedly a tone language... lexical tone is elusive though grammatical tone is still found in a few environments' (p. 41); posits two tones H/L with minimal pairs; tone not marked in orthography. Appendix A.1.2 (pp. 189-190) notes that Pichl 1967 transcribed '5 levels of tone along with 5 levels of stress', omitted from the new dictionary.
